entry.title: Restyling This Site With Codex
entry.content:
I am not really a frontend or UI person, but I do know how things work there.

I can tell when something feels wrong on a page, but that does not mean I always know the CSS responsible for it. This site is personal, though, so I care about how it feels. I want it to be simple, calm, and centred on the things I write.

I recently restyled it with Codex using GPT-5.6 Sol at high reasoning effort.

It started with a question about SEO. Then I noticed inconsistent spacing, duplicated CSS, mobile problems, and pages that did not feel related. What began as a review slowly became a restyling of almost the entire site.

I did not begin with a finished design or a detailed reconstruction plan. I moved through the site one page at a time. I questioned new files, asked why styles were duplicated, compared mobile screenshots, and sometimes reversed changes that felt like too much. The design emerged through those small decisions rather than from one large redesign.

Trying not to overdo it

An AI coding agent makes it very easy to add things. A page can quickly gain cards, borders, gradients, animations, and another stylesheet.

That speed is useful, but it can also produce too much design.

Some early changes looked cool but stopped feeling like my website. The About page was one example. It had more personality, but it also felt over-designed. I kept giving the same feedback:

Tone it down a bit.

Codex could produce and modify the interface quickly, while I decided what actually belonged. We would add something, look at it, and remove the parts that made the page feel busy.

The goal was never to turn the site into a modern landing page. I wanted a slightly better version of what was already here.

Minimal as a system

I started to think of minimalism as having fewer rules to remember, not just fewer things on the screen.

Links are blue and turn green when hovered. Writings, Notes, Paper, and their archives use the same visual language. Dates, tags, headings, lists, and the little cd navigation should not look as if they came from unrelated websites.

This meant sharing templates, using the existing Sass structure, removing duplicated code, and checking the same layouts on desktop and mobile. A new page can now inherit an existing pattern instead of needing its own design and stylesheet.

That is more useful to me than making one page impressive on its own.

The Daveads Galaxy

The biggest addition was the Daveads Galaxy: Daveads at the centre, categories as constellations, topics as planets, and articles inside them.

I did not want it to be a hardcoded visual that would break as I wrote more. It reads the categories and tags already used by Writings and Notes. When I publish something new, the Galaxy should understand where it belongs without me manually adding another planet.

Mobile made the feature more interesting. Planets needed useful touch targets. Tapping one had to reveal its articles. Zooming the Galaxy should not zoom the entire page, and the navigation still needed to work in full-screen mode. We also kept a list view for anyone who wants a simpler way to browse.

The Galaxy is more playful than the rest of the website, but it follows the same rule: content should drive the interface.

Working with Codex

A lot of my feedback came through screenshots. I would notice too much empty space, an uncentred video, a heading disappearing on mobile, or two labels sitting too close together. I could point at the problem without knowing which template or Sass rule created it.

Codex could trace the element back to the code and make a focused change. I would look at the result and decide whether it felt right. That loop worked well for someone who is not a frontend person but still has an opinion about the result.

We also checked the less visible things: responsiveness, builds, internal links, test pages, the Atom feed, and whether Google Analytics remained untouched.

After experimenting, we refactored the Galaxy into smaller files and shared common code across other pages. Generated code can work while still being difficult for a human to own. I want to open the repository later, find the relevant file, and change it myself.

GPT-5.6 Sol at high reasoning effort was helpful when a small request crossed templates, Sass, JavaScript, content configuration, and mobile behaviour. The official OpenAI documentation describes high effort as useful for complex planning, debugging, and agentic work, which matched this project.

But it did not replace taste. I still had to say when something was too much, protect the parts I liked, and ask whether a new file was really necessary.

Codex gave me implementation speed. I kept responsibility for what the website should feel like.

The site now has more capability, but its ordinary pages feel calmer and more consistent. More importantly, it still feels like mine.

entry.title: The Age of Infinite Software and Limited Imagination
entry.content:
We can build software faster than ever before.

You can describe an idea to an AI agent, give it a few instructions, and watch something that might have taken weeks or months begin taking shape in minutes.

You'd expect an explosion of creativity: more unusual ideas, ambitious experiments, and people attempting things that previously seemed impossible.

Yet sometimes I feel we're seeing the opposite.

Another AI wrapper. Another dashboard. Another application that looks remarkably similar to something that already exists.

Of course, people are doing genuinely interesting work. I'm not suggesting innovation has stopped. Maybe I'm just looking in the wrong places.

But I keep wondering:

If we now have some of the most powerful tools ever created, where is the spark?

Building isn't the same as imagining

There's a difference between being able to build something and imagining something worth building.

Generative AI is reducing the effort required to turn ideas into working systems. You don't necessarily need to understand every implementation detail before experimenting with an idea. That's incredible.

But making something easier to build doesn't automatically make us more imaginative. If we keep asking these systems to reproduce what already exists, why should we expect different outcomes?

I think we risk confusing productivity with creativity. Producing ten applications doesn't necessarily mean you've explored ten original ideas.

And perhaps that's where our thinking needs to change.

For a long time, much of our attention has gone into figuring out how to build things. As machines become increasingly capable of handling implementation, what happens to all that attention?

Do we simply produce more of the same things? Or do we start:

  • questioning assumptions,
  • connecting unrelated ideas, and
  • investigating problems we've accepted as normal?

What's stopping someone from vibe coding Google?

Here's something I've been thinking about.

What's stopping someone from opening Claude Code, Codex, or another coding agent and asking it to build Google? They'd need:

  • a web crawler,
  • a search index,
  • a ranking algorithm,
  • a query interface, and
  • perhaps even an advertising system.

Nothing is stopping them from trying, and they could probably build a functional search engine prototype surprisingly quickly.

But have they built Google? Not quite.

Google isn't simply a collection of source files. Behind its search engine are enormous infrastructure investments, continuously updated indexes, ranking systems, years of operational knowledge, and an entire ecosystem.

Writing software that resembles Google is one problem. Building something capable of competing with it at scale is another.

Are software moats really disappearing?

This is why I find the argument that software moats are disappearing somewhat incomplete.

Yes, writing code is becoming cheaper. Some products will become much easier to replicate, and some existing advantages will weaken.

But the value of a system has never been entirely about how difficult its code is to write. These still matter:

  • reliability,
  • architecture,
  • distribution,
  • accumulated knowledge, and
  • the ability to operate under real-world conditions.

None of these advantages is permanent. AI might eventually make many of them easier to reproduce, too.

But making something easier to build doesn't necessarily make it easy to replace.

The obsession to keep pushing

There's something else I think matters enormously: obsession.

Not necessarily spending endless hours writing code yourself, but having an almost unreasonable desire to understand a problem and keep pushing a system beyond its limitations.

Imagine two people with access to exactly the same AI tools.

The first asks an agent to build an application. It works, so they launch it and move on.

The second keeps questioning everything:

  • Why does it work this way?
  • Why does this limitation exist?
  • What happens if we change the architecture?
  • Could we approach the entire problem differently?

Both have the same tools, but they might produce radically different outcomes.

You might no longer need to implement every component manually, but you can still be the person directing the experiments, questioning the results, and deciding what to try next. And I find that fascinating.

Instead of spending weeks implementing a single approach, you might be able to investigate several alternatives, discover why they fail, and keep refining your understanding.

Of course, obsession alone isn't enough. You can spend years perfecting something nobody needs. But combine it with curiosity, technical understanding, judgment, and a willingness to experiment, and there's still something valuable there.

The first working implementation shouldn't necessarily be the end of your imagination. Sometimes it's where the interesting questions begin.

This goes beyond software

I don't think this opportunity is limited to software. Think about hardware, robotics, energy, manufacturing, or scientific research.

Imagine designing a robotic hand. You describe what you want, use AI to explore mechanical designs, simulate their movements, and generate components for a prototype. Eventually, you build one.

It works, but it struggles to pick up a tiny screw.

What happens next?

Do you accept the limitation, or do you start questioning the finger geometry, sensors, materials, and control system? Perhaps an entirely different mechanism would work better.

AI could help you investigate those possibilities, but someone still has to recognise the problem, test the ideas, and understand what the results mean.

And unlike software, the physical world has constraints that don't disappear because an AI generated a convincing design. Materials cost money. Components wear out. Manufacturing takes time. Physics doesn't care how impressive your prompt is.

Still, as these tools improve, individuals and smaller teams may gain the ability to attempt increasingly complex projects. There are machines we haven't invented, systems we haven't connected, and problems we haven't investigated deeply enough.

Not everything has to become another application.

A forced evolution in how we think?

I sometimes wonder whether we're approaching a point where a kind of forced evolution in our thinking becomes necessary. Not biological evolution, but a change in how we approach problems.

We've spent years learning how to use computers to accomplish tasks. Now computers are beginning to handle increasingly complex tasks on our behalf.

Perhaps this means we need to become more deliberate about exercising our creativity and logical reasoning: to ask better questions, challenge assumptions, and understand systems rather than merely operate them. To see possibilities where others see limitations.

I'm not suggesting that implementation no longer matters, or that technical understanding becomes irrelevant. Quite the opposite.

The better you understand something, the more effectively you can question it. And the more capable our tools become, the further those questions might take us.

But there's another possibility worth considering.

What if increasingly capable AI makes it easier for us to avoid thinking altogether?

We could become so comfortable accepting generated solutions that we stop investigating why they work, whether they're correct, or whether a better approach exists.

I don't think that's inevitable. But it's a choice we'll increasingly have to make.

Where is the spark?

There is still so much left to solve: healthcare, energy, robotics, biology, computing, and countless problems we probably haven't even recognised yet.

I don't think we're running out of ideas. I think we might be underestimating how much remains possible.

And perhaps the opportunity presented by generative AI isn't simply to build the same things faster. It's to explore things we previously couldn't afford to attempt.

We've made it easier than ever to turn an idea into something real. Maybe it's time we became more ambitious about the ideas themselves.

The machines are getting better at building. Are we getting better at imagining?

entry.title: How Merdra Handles Access to Medical Information
entry.content:
Medical information should follow a patient. That does not mean it should be open to every hospital, clinician, or application.

Medical records are confidential. A doctor, nurse, pharmacist, and physiotherapist may care for the same person, but they do not need the same access or have the same responsibilities. Access should depend on who is asking, why they are asking, what they need, and for how long.

Merdra is not a mirror of every hospital’s EMR. It is a trust and exchange layer for the parts of a medical history that need to move safely between care settings.

How access is decided

Patient permission is an important part of access, but it is not the only check.

Before Merdra returns a record, it should verify the:

  • Practitioner and organisation making the request
  • Role and purpose behind it
  • Requested scope and time limit
  • Applicable policy

Working at a hospital, or knowing a patient’s name, should not be enough to access their medical information.

What a patient can do

A patient should be able to:

  • See a patient-safe view of their Merdra history — what information Merdra holds, where it came from, when it was created, and whether it is current or corrected.
  • Choose who can retrieve relevant records — for example, approving a new hospital’s request for laboratory history for a defined purpose and period.
  • Revoke a sharing grant when it is no longer needed.
  • See access history — which organisation accessed which category of record and when.
  • Request a correction or add a patient statement when information appears wrong.

This does not mean a patient sees every raw internal hospital note or every result without context. Some information may require clinician discussion or be restricted under a defined safety and legal policy before appearing in the patient-facing view.

Patients cannot edit a diagnosis, prescription, or laboratory result. The organisation and professional who created a record remain accountable for it. A correction creates a new linked version while preserving the source and history.

What a treating provider can do

When a patient begins care at another hospital, an authorised provider can:

  • Request only what is needed for care.
  • State the purpose and duration of that request.
  • Retrieve a permitted, verified, source-attributed copy of the record.
  • Create new clinical information under their own organisation’s identity.

They cannot edit the original result, diagnosis, or note created elsewhere.

If Hospital B creates a new test result, diagnosis, or treatment record, that becomes Hospital B’s own clinical assertion. Merdra can add a structured and verifiable representation of it to the patient’s portable history.

What happens in an emergency?

There are situations where a patient may be unconscious or unable to approve access.

Merdra should eventually support a tightly controlled emergency-access path for verified clinicians. It should:

  • Expose only the information necessary for urgent care
  • Require a stated reason
  • Expire quickly
  • Create a full audit trail
  • Notify the patient afterwards, where appropriate

Emergency access must be a governed exception, not a back door into every patient record.

The principle

Hospitals keep using their local systems for appointments, billing, prescriptions, notes, and day-to-day care. Merdra does not replace or run those workflows. It handles the data layer:

  • Identity
  • Consent
  • Provenance
  • Permissions
  • Audit history
  • Safe exchange of selected medical information between authorised systems

Medical information should follow the patient without becoming a document that anyone can edit.

entry.title: What Is Merdra?
entry.content:
Health has a memory. Too often, healthcare does not.

When people move between clinics, hospitals, laboratories, or even cities, important parts of their medical history can be left behind. A test result may live on paper, in a PDF, in a WhatsApp chat, or inside a system that the next provider cannot access. At the next appointment, the conversation begins again: What happened before? Which medicines have you taken? Do you have the result?

The problem is not that clinicians do not care about context. It is that the systems around them rarely allow reliable health information to travel with the person it belongs to.

That is the problem Merdra exists to solve.

Merdra is health-data infrastructure

Merdra is building the trust and interoperability layer that lets medical information follow a patient.

We are not trying to become every hospital's electronic medical-record system, nor are we building another place to upload documents and forget them. We are building the underlying infrastructure that can help laboratories, healthcare providers, patient applications, and future clinical tools work from health information that is structured, permissioned, and trustworthy.

We are also building Merdra so other healthcare startups and developers can build their own applications on it.

In simple terms, Merdra should make it possible for the right health information to be available to the right person or system, at the right time, with the patient's permission.

Why records today are not enough

Most healthcare information is created for a moment: a consultation, a prescription, a test, or a discharge. But a person's health is not a series of isolated moments. It is a continuing story.

When that story is fragmented, every new provider has to reconstruct it. Patients must remember details under pressure, carry documents around, or repeat tests that may already have been done. Providers make decisions with less context than they should have. And valuable information that could support better care stays trapped in formats and systems that cannot easily work together.

The consequences of fragmented history are not abstract. In Medical History, we shared conversations with two doctors on our team about the difficulty of retrieving older records and using information from elsewhere during care.

Digitising a document alone does not solve this. A scanned result is easier to store, but it is still difficult for software and often for another provider to understand, compare, or safely use.

Merdra is being built so health data can be more than a collection of files.

What Merdra makes possible

At its core, Merdra brings together a few things healthcare data needs in order to be useful across systems:

  • Structured information. Important clinical details such as a lab test's name, value, unit, reference range, and date should be represented as data, not just as pixels on a page.
  • Provenance. A record should show where it came from, who created it, and when. That gives the next person or system a basis for understanding whether it can be trusted.
  • Consent and access control. Health information is deeply personal. Patients should be able to understand and control how it is shared, while providers get the information they are authorised to use.
  • Interoperability. Different organisations and applications should not need to start from zero every time they need to work together. With permission, they should be able to exchange relevant information in a reliable way.
  • An audit trail. Access and changes should be accountable. Trust cannot be an afterthought when the data concerns someone's health.

These capabilities may sound technical, but their purpose is human: to give patients continuity, give clinicians context, and make safer, more useful health software possible.

We are starting with lab results

Merdra's first focus is structured diagnostic laboratory results.

Lab results are a practical place to begin because they are important, common, and often difficult to carry from one point of care to another. They also contain the kind of precise information that becomes far more useful when it is structured: a result can be compared over time, interpreted alongside other records, or shared with a new provider without someone having to manually re-enter it.

The first milestone is not to capture every piece of medical information at once. It is to create a trustworthy path for a laboratory result to become a portable, usable record—one a patient can access and share, and one an authorised provider or tool can understand.

From there, Merdra can expand carefully toward a more complete longitudinal health history: medication records, diagnoses, care events, and other information that helps tell the full story.

Trust is the product

Health data is not ordinary data. It can affect a diagnosis, a treatment decision, a person's privacy, and their confidence in the healthcare system.

That means Merdra has to be built around trust from the beginning. Information needs clear provenance. Sharing needs meaningful consent. Access needs accountability. And interoperability cannot come at the cost of patient dignity or security.

The goal is not simply to move more data around. It is to make the data that moves understandable, traceable, and appropriately controlled.

Beyond continuity: building clinical context

Continuity is the first promise, not the final value. A record that can move with a patient is useful; a trustworthy longitudinal history can also help people and software understand what has changed, what may be connected, and what information is still missing.

As Merdra's records become more structured and longitudinal, we can support clinician-facing tools that surface trends over time, relevant medication and diagnostic history, family-health context, and gaps or contradictions in the record. Each signal should make its basis visible: the source records, the dates, the units, and the limits of what is known.

This is not about asking software to make a diagnosis on its own. It is about giving clinicians clearer, source-grounded context so they can apply their judgement. Over time, validated clinical decision-support and preventive tools may be built on this foundation. But trustworthy data, meaningful consent, transparency, and human review have to come first.

Family context deserves particular care. Knowing relevant family history is not the same as having access to another person's private medical record.

Building from Nigeria, with a global ambition

We are starting in Nigeria, where fragmented records, paper workflows, PDFs, and disconnected providers make the need for continuity especially clear. But this is not only a Nigerian problem. Around the world, healthcare is still organised around institutions while people's lives and health needs move across them.

Nigeria is Merdra's beachhead, not its boundary.

We want to prove the model where the problem is real and urgent, learn directly from patients, laboratories, and providers, and build infrastructure strong enough to support healthcare wherever people need their information to move with them.

A foundation for the next generation of care

Better health software and eventually responsible clinical intelligence depends on better underlying information. AI cannot responsibly fill the gaps created by missing, unverified, or disconnected records. It needs data that is structured, longitudinal, permissioned, and traceable.

Merdra is building toward that future, but it begins with a much simpler promise: your health information should not be trapped where it was created.

It should be able to follow you, with context and with your permission.

entry.title: Medical History
entry.content:
When you visit a doctor, the conversation usually begins with what is bothering you now. But understanding your current condition can also mean looking at what happened before.

A previous diagnosis, a medicine you are taking, an operation, or a reaction to treatment may influence the decisions made during that visit. Your medical history gives the doctor context for understanding the person in front of them.

I wanted to understand how this works in everyday practice, so I asked doctors on our team how they use previous patient information and what happens when they cannot access it. This article draws on two of those conversations.

Their responses brought the problem into focus. Sometimes patients can explain their history clearly. Sometimes they cannot. And sometimes the information has already been recorded, but the doctor still has difficulty retrieving it.

When the record exists but can't be reached

One doctor described a consultation that illustrated this last situation.

The patient could not clearly explain an existing diagnosis or name the medicines they were taking. The facility had recently moved to a different electronic medical record system. To understand the patient's treatment and decide what needed to change, the doctor and a consultant had to pause the consultation and retrieve information from the old system.

The information existed. Finding it still interrupted the care being provided.

The clinician still needs to assess the person in front of them. Previous documentation contributes to that assessment alongside the patient's account, examination findings, and relevant investigations.

When there is no record at all

Both doctors said that when records are unavailable, they take a fresh history. One pointed out that this can be straightforward when the patient can clearly describe their health and treatment. Missing documentation does not make every consultation impossible.

The difficulty becomes more apparent when the person cannot provide that account. The other doctor described an unconscious patient whose relatives did not know about an existing condition. Important parts of the patient's history became clear only during further assessment.

What patients and families carry

Those experiences made me think about how much we ask patients and families to carry between appointments. Imagine arriving at a new clinic with results on your phone, a prescription on paper, and details of an earlier consultation you are trying to remember.

Someone may know they take a tablet without knowing its name. A relative may accompany a patient without knowing their earlier diagnoses. A record can help fill those gaps, while still needing to be checked against the patient's current situation.

Medication history

Medication information was another concrete example. One doctor described how reviewing a patient's medication history led the team to postpone a planned operation. I am keeping the clinical details general here, but the significance for this discussion is clear: information about earlier care changed the next decision.

Accurate medication records include:

  • current medicines,
  • known allergies and reactions, and
  • changes to treatment.

The Care Quality Commission's guidance also emphasises checking discrepancies when people move between care settings.

Why investigations get repeated

The conversations also changed how I think about investigations. Not every consultation requires new laboratory tests or access to every past record. What matters is whether the available information helps answer the current clinical question.

Even when an earlier result is available, another test may be needed. The doctors described several different reasons for repeating an investigation:

  • Monitoring: a new result may be needed to assess changes in the patient's condition or response to treatment.
  • Checking a finding: a result that raises concerns about reliability or differs substantially from the clinical picture may prompt further investigation.
  • Missing information: a previous result may have to be repeated because it cannot be retrieved.

Those reasons deserve separate attention. Better access could help address the third situation. It would not remove the need for clinical monitoring or for questioning a result.

A result needs context

A value outside a reference range does not always indicate illness, and a value within it does not always rule illness out. Interpretation depends on the wider clinical picture.

Earlier results may help reveal changes over time. Dates, units, reference ranges, and testing methods matter when making comparisons. Results from different laboratories may not be directly comparable.

For anyone building software around medical records, those details deserve as much attention as the number itself.

Trusting results from elsewhere

That leads to another question I asked: what makes a doctor trust a result from another facility?

Both doctors discussed the facility's track record and whether the findings made sense alongside the patient's presentation. Their accounts suggest that access and confidence in the information are separate problems to understand.

For Merdra, that distinction matters. Recording where a result came from and whether it has changed can make its history traceable. It does not, by itself, establish that the test was performed correctly or that the interpretation is accurate.

When an institution changes software

The old-EMR example raises a related engineering question. What happens to a patient's history when an institution changes software? In the case described to me, the clinicians could retrieve it, but doing so required an extra step during the consultation. Making information digital had not made continuity automatic.

Both doctors wanted reliable access to previous records across facilities. My interpretation is that continuity should mean access to relevant information in a form the clinician can assess and use. It needs to be current enough for the decision and available to the people authorised to use it. Patients should not have to surrender privacy to benefit from continuity.

What we are building

This is part of the problem we are working on at Merdra.

We are building towards medical information that can follow a patient across providers and become usable by other healthcare software. Identity, permissions, and the source and history of each record are part of that foundation.

Making information available is one part of the work. Its accuracy, meaning, and place in the clinical workflow matter too.

These conversations give us specific things to investigate as we build:

  • how clinicians retrieve older records,
  • how they check results from elsewhere, and
  • where information becomes difficult to use.

We still need to learn how often these situations occur and whether our approach helps in practice.

The question I want us to keep asking is simple:

When someone needs care, can the people caring for them access and understand the information that matters?

Note:

Paraphrased from responses shared by two doctors on the Merdra team while developing this article. These are exploratory conversations, not a representative study. Patient and facility identifiers are not included.

entry.title: The Kind of Founder I Aim to Be
entry.content:
When I think about finding investors, I also think about the conversations we will have after they back us.

A year later:

  • What would they say about working with me?
  • Would they understand where their money went?
  • Would they understand the progress we had made, what we had learned, and the challenges we were facing?
  • Would they feel that I had taken their belief in me seriously?

Those questions matter to me.

I live in Nigeria. Building a company from here means working through constraints, including distance from many of the people I hope to build relationships with. There are fewer opportunities for someone on the other side of the world to meet me casually or watch how I work over time.

That makes me think carefully about how I make my work visible, explain my decisions, and earn trust.

I want to build relationships that last for years. I want to earn the trust of the people who back me through the way I work and the commitments I keep, so they are willing to listen when I bring them another difficult problem worth solving.

That starts with how I handle the opportunity in front of me.

For me, keeping my word starts with being careful about what I promise. If I say an investment will help us reach a particular milestone, I should be able to explain the work involved, the assumptions behind the plan, and how we will measure progress. I should understand the terms I agree to and take those commitments seriously.

Those commitments should remain visible in how I run the company.

I want to be deliberate about who we hire, what we prioritise, and how we use capital. Each decision should have a clear purpose, with progress we can assess. I will take responsibility for the results, address mistakes early, and act on what we learn, even when that means changing a decision I strongly believed in.

Communication matters just as much when the news is difficult. A delayed product, a customer who walks away, or an assumption that turns out to be wrong should lead to an honest conversation. People who have backed me should have enough information to understand the situation.

Building Merdra will mean developing new ideas and refining our approach as we learn. Research can challenge a plan. Customers can reveal a different problem. When that happens, I want to explain the evidence, discuss the consequences, and agree on any necessary changes to our commitments.

I cannot promise that every decision will work. I'm committed to doing the work, taking responsibility for my decisions, and being truthful about the results.

My focus now is Merdra. I want to build infrastructure that allows medical information to follow a patient across healthcare providers and become useful to the software built around their care.

My vision for Merdra is ambitious. Software is our focus today, and over time I want us to expand into hardware that works with the infrastructure we are building. Getting there will take sustained work. I want us to earn each next step through what we build, learn, and deliver today.

A lasting investor relationship will still require each new idea to stand on its own merits. What I hope carries forward is a clear record of how I work.

Years from now, I would like someone introducing me to be able to say: "He takes his commitments seriously, he tells you what is happening, and he keeps doing the difficult work."

I want to earn that description through the way I build Merdra.

entry.title: Outsourcing your brain
entry.content:
Once upon a time I used to Imagine the power one person could hold if they truly understood how technology works.

Now, that idea feels a bit shaky because thinking has been outsourced to LLMs.

But using your brain is just as important as going to the gym, it’s how you stay mentally strong.

It’s okay to be clueless or make unhealthy decisions at some point in your life, just make sure you start using your brain before it’s too late.

It’s important you take note of how new technology affects you.

  • Learn how to learn //learn to push your self
  • Understand how thing works on a deeper level.

Be the control freak to LLm...

Learn to use your brain.

At some point in the future, thinking might just be the next new thing.

entry.title: My Approach to Resting Right from the Gym
entry.content:
One thing you shouldn't do when aiming to take a rest is to spend more than a month resting. You are pretty much reversing all that hard work. I am actually known as the guy that can never take a rest from the gym...

Spoilers
I once told @soso and @Retr0ville that I was going to take a break from the gym for a week and ended up going to two gym sessions during the same week. Weird, right? :) //There are a couple more examples.


How would I take a proper rest assuming I am willing to take a one-month rest?

entry.title: The Linux Command line interface(0)
entry.content:
I spend 90% of my time in the Terminal emulator (not really sure about that tho), for me it offer's great flexibility and control than the GUI, and it can be really intimidating at first but it worth your time.

Prerequisites: unix or unix-like operating system.

Goals:

  • Learn what a command line is and how to use it
  • Learn common useful commands and what they mean

What a command line interface?

when talking about the command line we are actually refering to The Shell. The shell is a program that takes in Commands or #keywords and passes them to the operating system to carry out. it's a way of interacting with the computer os, similiar to the GUI but faster and more powerful. The program which handles this commands in the terminal emulator is the Command-line interpreter (shell).

Shell Scripting:

As earlier said a Unix shell or shell is a command-line interpreter but also a programming language, the programming language features allows us to combine commands or (utilities) together in a file and run them as a scripts, and yea you can also call it a Script language for now the major focus is getting you to understand the command line and having the feels of it without getting intimidated.. will write more on Shell script on Using The Linux Command Line(1) or probably the next.

Running the Termainal emulator:

Computer terminal:

Before delving into what the Terminal emulator actually is, it's important to know where it all started decades ago. Computers had no GUI for accessing or modifying data; the computer terminal was the only means of entering, displaying, and printing data. These terminals were physical computing devices like IBM 3270, VT100, and many others. For more details, check out computer terminal >> wiki.

What's a Terminal emulator: The Terminal emulator is a software designed to replicate the functions of a computer terminal. It is a GUI application needed to access the Unix shell environment, providing an interface to invoke commands, scripts, and programs available on your system. It also allows you to view and browse through the contents of directories, just like you would with a FILE MANAGER APPLICATION.

Every Linux distro comes with a default terminal emulator. For instance, Ubuntu and Fedora come with Gnome terminal emulator, and other Linux distros have their own defaults. The first thing you see in the terminal emulator is the "command prompt," which shows $, %, #, or >, indicating the current working directory, the current user, and the readiness of the shell to accept commands from you.

The default shell for most Unix or Unix-like systems is the bash shell. Other shells include sh, zsh, csh, and more. To find out the available shells on your system, use the command:

cat /etc/shells

Display content in your file directory

The ls command is used to print out the current directory on the terminal emulator screen, giving the same result as the File Manager.

To find out what a command means through the command line, type:

whatis ls

You can also make use of the system's manual pager for the full documentation:

man ls

To print your current working directory, use the command pwd.

The pwd is a built-in command within the bash shell itself. Type help to find out more about built-in commands.

Time for Experiments

Here are some common commands:

CommandMeaning
lsList files and directories in the current directory.
cdChange the current working directory.
pwdPrint the current working directory.
mkdirCreate a new directory (folder).
rmdirRemove a directory (folder).
cpCopy files or directories.
mvMove or rename files or directories.
rmRemove (delete) files or directories.
catConcatenate and display file content.
moreDisplay file content one screen at a time.
lessDisplay file content with backward navigation.
headDisplay the beginning lines of a file.
tailDisplay the ending lines of a file.
grepSearch for a pattern in files.
findSearch for files and directories.
chmodChange file permissions.
chownChange file ownership.
psDisplay information about running processes.
killTerminate processes.
sshSecure Shell - remote login to a server.
wgetDownload files from the web.
tarArchive files using tar.
zipPackage and compress files.

Please note that this is not an exhaustive list, but it includes some commonly used commands and their primary meanings. Additionally, the meaning of some commands may vary based on their options and arguments. Always refer to the manual (man command) for a comprehensive understanding of each command.

entry.title: Technological Innovation in developing countries
entry.content:
Note: These are based on my views on factors affecting the rate of innovation in developing countries. I might be wrong, but at the same time, I might be right.

Writing this article feels a little weird for me; it seems like something I should not write about, but I also have the feeling that I should do it anyway. Keeping this as short as possible, I won't be able to cover all areas.

People in developing countries seem to believe that the governing entities are solely responsible for bringing about technological innovation (this is done indirectly), which is something I strongly disagree with. I guess I am not expressing this in the right way; coming from a tech background, there is a lot I don't fully understand about politics. It's not an excuse, but rather than complaining, that energy should be directed towards something else.

Secondly, the mindset (culture) and beliefs of the people are really mind-blowing. I love this quote: "You are what you believe in." It's really funny how, at the age of 20-25 in most cases, you are still considered incapable of making decisions that could cause a serious change in society, down to individual families, and this becomes a loop.

It makes me wonder what the adults spend their youthful age doing in their 20's....??? This makes me want to give examples of Bill Gates, Steve Jobs, Mark Zuckerberg...

To a point, you can't entirely blame society for this; many youths spend their time in the most unproductive ways you could ever think of, involving themselves in internet fraud and other criminal activities, etc.

There is a lot at play here:

  1. Lack of knowledge, even in a major field (poor education background, mostly outdated curriculum).
  2. Lack of infrastructure, etc.

Technological innovation can be brought about by innovative individuals (Tech Visionaries) who:

x. See things differently.
x. Have a serious, intense passion for what they do.
x. Are ready to take action no matter the odds.
x. Are tired of doing things the old way (with low outcomes).
x. Are highly curious (question everything) and have the ability to connect the dots.

Don't get me wrong, one person can't actually change the world; you are going to work together with intelligent humans and people who think alike to actually make a mark.

entry.title: Indentation in Python
entry.content:
what is indentation:

According to wikipedia - indentation indent is an empty space at the beginning of a line to signal the start of a new paragraph.

In Python indentation refers to the (spaces and tabs) that are used at the beginning of a statement, it is a way of telling the interpreter this part of the code belongs to the same group,in programming language like c, c++, java, kotlin.. curly braces {} are use to indicate the start and end of a block of code..

indentation in java

public class indentation{ 
	public static void main(String[] args)
		{ // shows this is the body of the main method
		
		Scanner input = new Scanner(System.in);
		out.println("input a valid password")
		String user_input = input.next();

		if (user_input.equals("evad")){ // if statement body     
			out.println("logged in \n");
		}  
		else{
			out.println("incorrect password\n");
		}
	} //end of the main method
} //end of the of the porgramm

Question: what's the whole point of indentation ?
Answer: glance through the example below and tell me what you think about it.

The coherence theory states that a proposition is true if and only if that proposition coheres with the other propositions that one believes. . . . The problem with the coherence theory is that a belief could be consistent with my other beliefs and yet the whole lot could be false. —Colin McGinn (2015a, p. 148) According to the coherence theory of truth (see Young 2018), a set of propositions (or beliefs, or sentences) is true iff:they are mutually consistent, and 2.they are supported by, or consistent with, all available evidence; that is, they “cohere” with each other and with all evidence. Note that observation statements (that is, descriptions of what we observe in the world around us) are among the claims that must be mutually consistent, so this is not (necessarily) a “pie-in-the-sky” theory that doesn’t have to relate to the way things really are. It just says that we don’t have to have independent access to “reality” in order to determine truth. 2.4.3Correspondence vs. Coherence Which theory is correct? Well, for one thing, there are more than two theories: There are several versions of each kind of theory, and there are other theories of truth that don’t fall under either category. The most important of the other theories is the “prag- matic” theory of truth (see Glanzberg 2016, §3; Misak and Talisse 2019). Here is one version: [T]he pragmatic theory of truth . . . is that a proposition is true if and only [if] it is useful [that is, “pragmatic”, or practical] to believe that proposi- tion. (McGinn, 2015a, p. 148, my interpolated brackets) Another version states that a belief, proposition, or sentence is true iff it continues to be accepted at the limit of inquiry: Truth is that to which a belief would tend were it to tend indefinitely to a fixed belief. (Edwin Martin, Jr., paraphrasing C.S. Peirce; lectures on the theory of knowledge,Spring 1973; for more on Peirce, see §2.6.1.3,below.)46

Indentation in python is very important because with out proper indenting you will end up seeing IndentationError: examples as seen below

print("not true")

    print("same")
    print("same")

a = 0;
b = 10
while(a <= 10):
